hypotheses.observation: The structural candidate covers 42% of the measured target workload and has a derived upper-bound speedup of 1.30.
hypotheses.mechanism: Reducing time in the dominant block-level data path can affect a substantial fraction of total local-workload execution time.
hypotheses.transformation: Evaluate the structural transformation on the dominant block-level data path.
preconditions: The measured 42% fraction remains representative of the target deployment workload.
The 1.30 speedup bound is attainable without adding comparable overhead.
Correctness and resource-usage behavior are preserved.
hypotheses.expected_effect: Potential local-workload speedup is materially larger than for the micro candidate; the idealized bound from the supplied fraction and speedup is approximately 1.17x overall.
risks: The measured local-workload fraction may not represent deployment mix.
Transformation overhead or resource pressure may reduce the realized benefit.
The derived speedup is an upper bound, not a measured result.
required_evidence: End-to-end timing on representative deployment workloads before and after the transformation.
Validation of resource usage and correctness.

hypotheses.observation: The micro candidate has an 8.0x derived upper-bound speedup but applies to only 0.2% of execution in one small auxiliary kernel.
hypotheses.mechanism: The small affected fraction limits whole-workload impact despite a large local speedup bound.
hypotheses.transformation: Defer or separately measure the micro-kernel transformation rather than treating its local speedup as a whole-workload benefit.
preconditions: The 0.2% fraction is representative of the workload being optimized.
The candidate does not materially reduce time outside the measured kernel.
hypotheses.expected_effect: Even at its supplied upper bound, the idealized whole-local-workload gain is only about 0.18%, so the practical impact is expected to be small unless workload mix differs substantially.
risks: The kernel fraction may vary across deployment workloads.
Optimization overhead could outweigh the bounded benefit.
Focusing on this candidate could delay evaluation of the dominant data path.
unknowns: Whether the auxiliary kernel becomes dominant in another workload.
required_evidence: Per-kernel timing across representative deployment workloads.

hypotheses.observation: The two candidates touch disjoint execution regions, but the recorded fractions are only for the target local workload and deployment mix is unknown.
hypotheses.mechanism: Disjoint regions permit separate attribution in a first-order timing model, while workload-mix uncertainty prevents reliable deployment-level ranking.
hypotheses.transformation: Measure representative deployment workload composition and evaluate each candidate independently and in combination.
preconditions: The regions remain disjoint under the tested workload.
Timing measurements can isolate both regions.
hypotheses.expected_effect: The measurements will distinguish whether the structural candidate remains dominant, whether the micro candidate matters for another workload, and whether their combined effect is close to the first-order model.
risks: Workload-dependent interactions may invalidate simple additive modeling.
Measurement noise may obscure a sub-percent micro benefit.
The supplied local fractions may not generalize.
required_evidence: Per-region and end-to-end timing for each candidate alone and together.
Validation that the execution regions remain disjoint.
